projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Thomas Stillisano was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran, Thomas P. Stillisano. Mr. Stillisano served in the U.S. Army with the 43rd Division. He served in the Pacific theater, and his highest rank was corporal. I'm Tom Swope and this recording was made at Mr. Stillisano's home in Euclid, Ohio, on March 15, 2002. Mr. Stillisano's wife was also present, and Tom was 83 at the time of this recording. What was your home town when the war started?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: Willoughby, Ohio.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you sign up or were you drafted?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: I was drafted.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When was that?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: '41, wasn't it?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: '43, that's right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How old were you then?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: 21, I think I was.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Stillisano
sp.p: 25, about 25.

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: 25. See, my wife has to correct me. I don't remember.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Stillisano
sp.p: He's 83 years old; you don't remember.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I'll do the math. I have some forms here. If you have your discharge papers you can put the information on there. So, were you anxious to jump in after the Japanese attacked Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: No. I was drafted; I had one kid.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, you did have a kid at the time?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So it took a little bit longer to draft you?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: I had a -- I was working at White Motors (ph), and they gave me a deferment twice. Then they called me. Couldn't get no more deferments.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You were drafted into the marines?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: No, the army.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The army; okay.

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: Drafted in the army.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: My notes are wrong.

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: And I went in there. I didn't care. After I was drafted, I didn't care. You had to go, so I went.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So what can you tell me about basic training?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: Went to Camp Perry for basic training and I was in the kitchen for 18 hours slicing bacon. That was interesting. I was slicing bacon. Boy, I was walking back to my barracks still slicing it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Got used to that repetitive motion?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So that was in Camp Perry?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: Camp Perry, then they shifted us to Mississippi--Camp McCain, I think it was.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Stillisano
sp.p: After Mississippi you went to California.

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: Then they shipped us, give us all winter clothes, new things, we went to California. We had to turn those clothes in there. We got summer clothes. As we were driving along, everybody -- I was the acting sergeant, and I had a bottle of CC with me and everybody was waiting, so finally I pulled a bottle out and asked if anybody wanted a drink. There was about six more bottles there the guys had. They was afraid to pull them out because I was the acting sergeant. But, then when I got to Camp Perry, I was back to buck private. Then, that was when they shipped us to California. It wasn't bad. I didn't mind it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How long were you in California then?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: Jeez, I don't know. Could have been there about two, three months. Then they went to Texas. Camp Bowie?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Stillisano
sp.p: You went to Texas first, then California, then the Pacific, New Guinea and the Philippines, Tommy, remember?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: Then we got shifted over to the Philippines. And it was a little rough, sleeping outside in them tents, and you could hear Washing Machine Charlie come over the night, bombing the place. But didn't hit anything. But I was waiting for them to hit the bank. That's where all the money was at.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That was the camp bank?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: Yeah, the camp bank. Army bank. But they missed that, too. Didn't hit nothing. But they come about three or four nights in a row. They couldn't hit nothing.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That was a single airplane that would fly over at night?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: Yeah. They called it Washing Machine Charlie. And I got in my trench I had dug, and there was a snake and I didn't care about bullets or nothing, I got out of that trench to see what was going on.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Stillisano
sp.p: Poor Tommy. He hates snakes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: And it was all right, though.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your unit?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: 671st Engineers. I don't know. We were doing all right but--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your job, your specific job?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: Surveyor. I was -- we was surveying for, we would put the artillery guns in position. And that was quite a job but we got everything straightened out pretty well. Everybody worked together. Then we had a topographical engineering in our outfit, in our company, draw maps, surveyed the ground. And, I don't know, what the heck.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember about when you went overseas?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: No. I have no idea.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was it maybe '44?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Stillisano
sp.p: He was overseas -- oh yeah, he never come back home till '46. It was almost '47 because it was the middle of December. Then January was coming. He was a corporal when he come home.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your first stop overseas then?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: Surveying.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where was the first place you went to?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: (?Finch Haven?)

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where is that?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: New Guinea.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have any specific memories of New Guinea?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: No. It was just a jungle. That's all.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: It was just a jungle?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: In New Guinea, it's just jungles. And we seen, come across one of those big snakes, about 20 feet long and he come by and his jaws opened wide like that. I didn't sleep for two nights. I was waiting for the rest of the family to come in. But, they caught it and they tried to scare me. Which I was scared of snakes and four guys were holding it, so I had this machete knife. I says, one of you is going to come by me too close, and there's going to be one or two heads are going to go. I had that machete. I was swinging it; I was going to hit whoever put it close to me. I didn't care who it was. When I told the company commander you better get rid of that snake or you're going to lose a sergeant. But they had him get rid of it.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Stillisano
sp.p: Remember the Philippines--the captain--because you didn't have your shirt on, Tommy?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: Oh, yeah. I got gigged in the Philippines, too.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What's "gigged"?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: I got -- I stopped to help a lieutenant. I was in a jeep going down. His jeep broke down. So I stopped to give him a hand, get him started again and we got him started and we get to camp, he -- how do you say it -- he gigged me for not having my shirt on. So I got three days cutting grass at the Filipino presidential, the big holding they had there, cutting grass for three days. That was pretty nice. These Filipino kids come over, they wanted to try it. I let them cut it. But then they stopped me. They said, "You cut it, not the kids."

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You have any other vivid memories of the Philippines?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: Not much, no.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What were the people like?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: They were all right. They all had long hair like the Beatles. That's where I think the United States got the idea from the Beatles, in the Philippines with the long hair.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Had the Japanese been driven out of the Philippines at that point or were they still there?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: There was some there. Some islands. I was walking down with a transit (ph) on my shoulder, coming down a hill and here this Filipino comes out of a cave, and I thought it was a Japanese. I was ready to shoot him. But found out he was a Filipino. I let him go. But he could have got shot come running out of that cave. They look like Japanese. What the hell. I was going to give him a good slice of the rifle I had. That's about it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was the next stop after the Philippines then?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Stillisano
sp.p: You went to Japan, didn't you?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: We went to Japan, yeah, but there was nothing going there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That was the occupying forces?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: Yeah. She knows more than I do.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But you probably got a lot of letters. If you want to get close to the microphone and talk about anything you remember.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Stillisano
sp.p: All I can say is that when he left, my daughter was six months old and when he came back she was three and a half years old. So I had it pretty rough there for a while.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you send pictures and updates?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Then sometimes I wouldn't hear from him for six weeks or more and then he'd finally write, and he would say I couldn't write because I was moved some place else, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What kinds of things could he write to you?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: There was stuff that was scratched off a lot.

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: Mail was censored.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Stillisano
sp.p: Mail was censored so there was a lot of things that was blacked out. Say, he would try to tell me where he was going or something like that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: I did get four battle stars, you know. I got four of those and one bronze arrow, bronze arrow star. And I got the medal -- how do you call it -- the bronze star.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was that for?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: We were knocking out an artillery nest by us. Knocked them all out. Or else we'd have got -- but you had to be careful where you was going. Three other guys and myself got the bronze star. And I didn't know I was getting it until I got home.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was the bronze arrow for? This was for an invasion?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Which invasion would that have been for?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: See that's the three brown and beiges and this is the bronze star. And I had a good conduct and I had sharp shooters.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So the arrow was for which invasion?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: I don't know. If we put four, we got that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So what four campaign were you involved in?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: Philippines.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: New Guinea?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: Yeah. New Guinea, the Philippines, Leyte and I forget what was--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What's this stripe?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: Technician.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Is this T-five, technician fifth grade?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's what my dad was eventually, at the very end. So you have any other vivid memories of those campaigns?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: No. Just that we had those battles and it was bad going into them. You didn't know what you was getting into, you know. They were shooting in all directions.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Stillisano
sp.p: Then you thought you were going to see Pat.

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: My brother was a lieutenant. I was supposed to get two weeks vacation, and I was supposed to go over there, but they pulled us out and I couldn't go see him. But he was waiting for me to go see him over there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have any particular memories of buddies?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: Oh, yeah. I had good buddies. I had one kid, his name was Norton. I give him the name of Mistronowski (ph). My god, that name stuck with him through all the time. We had these reunions; he would get up there--he was a real buddy to me. Then I had another guy, he was really scared. Well, I was scared too. I wasn't a brave hero; I was scared a lot of times, but this guy --

sp.speaker: Mrs. Stillisano
sp.p: Shuper (ph)was scared.

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: Shuper (ph). This guy was always scared about something. But I cured him up where he got along all right then. Because a lot of guys, they were away from home, like I was away, didn't realize what we were getting into. But, we had a good time. I'd give a dance once in a while. A Hula dance in New Guinea. I would have a wig.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Stillisano
sp.p: Grass skirts and--tell him about the reunions that we had, but now they're slowing down.

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: They're all dying. We don't have that many guys any more. We used to have reunions every year--Angola, Indiana. Now they changed it to some place else, but I don't like to drive nights. I'll be 84 years old my next birthday. I don't want to, I don't want to take the chance at night. I'm not as alert as I used to be.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Stillisano
sp.p: There are about 50, 60 guys that you were in the service with that are dead now. Because we would get the newsletter.

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: We only have about 20 guys left. But they're going to have it at another place that's closer, but I'm not going to go. I would like to go, but--

sp.speaker: Mrs. Stillisano
sp.p: Botkins in Ohio. No, that place where the airplane, Armstrong.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where Neil Armstrong was from?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: Where they had his astronaut thing.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Down there near Dayton somewhere? That's not too bad a drive. You could drive in the daylight.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Stillisano
sp.p: Yeah, when we went, we left in the daytime and stayed over night and left in the morning.

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: I don't know. I'm debating. This is a new area now. And I'm debating about going, but I don't think I'm going to make it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you talked about that guy that was scared; what did you do to cheer him up?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: I cheered him up, had him smile, told a little joke here and there, and he was scared. He was never home, I mean he was never away from home. This was the first time. He was younger than me. Finally, I got him to be happy and smiling and he was doing real good afterwards. Then I had another one that was a little scared, too. They were in the jungle. They were shooting the rifle between the--at a helmet and a bullet ricochetted, came back and hit him in the eye, lost an eye, one guy. Like a bullet went in the helmet, shoot right back at him. You wouldn't believe it. You would think it would go through it. What is it? That little --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were they shooting at this empty helmet for target practice?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: Yeah. Just fooling around. Shooting at that helmet and it just ricochetted right around and hit him. We had an Indian in our outfit. He was something. Chief Fool-some (ph) they called him. He could sneak up behind you and you wouldn't hear him. He was a real Indian from Oklahoma. Hell of a nice guy. I got along with him -- matter of fact, I got along with everybody. I was stuck in there, I didn't care as long as I got to come home, that was the only thing I figured but it didn't bother me. After you're in there a couple of months, you got used to it. And this other kid got hit in the eye and he lost his eyes (sic) and he said, "Oh, my god, I'll never be able to see my twins." I think he had twin girls when he was in the army, but he never seen them until he got home. But only his one eye was bad. He got a glass eye, too -- Bodine (ph). That's about it. I don't know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember what you might have done for entertainment other than the little shows you put on?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: I would put on little shows--I would get a grass skirt, we would do the Hula. One time we went to a Filipino party. It was more or less the same thing. Everybody got together, had a good time in there. But you never had many good parties, never. Because you were always on the run.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have a record player, phonograph or anything?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: No, no. They might have had a record player but it was just some old one, wasn't worth a damn.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any USO shows come around?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: No. We never seen no USO shows. We just traveled around different islands. Saipan. That would be the other--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That would be the other one. There we go.

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: Yeah. Saipan, I got it there. That wasn't a bad place. They were all moved out of there. The Japanese moved out, but they were hiding in there. They didn't move out; they were supposed to been gone. But you would get these snipers at night, up in a coconut tree. You had to be careful.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How did you flush them out there?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: You would hear and watch. We all looked up -- but they was hiding pretty good. It was hard to catch them. But I don't know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How about when you were in the occupying forces in Japan? What was that like?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: It was all right. I got a haircut for a quarter and a shave for fifteen cents. The Japanese -- they were good friends and the Filipinos, they were good too. But the Japanese, I don't think they knew what the hell was going-- but the war was over, too, you know, and they was glad it was over, too. Because a lot of them got killed. You would be walking along the highway there, and you would see them laying in the ditches, these Japanese, flies. Before they had a chance to bury them, I guess, or haul them away.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were the people pretty nice?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: Yeah. They were afraid of us when we pulled up there in the big trucks, everybody with their helmets and rifles. They would all look out the window, out the grass shack, to see what we were going to do, shoot or what, but after they seen us, they come out, they bowed, they were happy we were there. A lot of kids were getting killed; not only soldiers, but they was killing anything that moved. It was all right. I didn't mind it a bit after I got in there. It didn't bother me a bit.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you think of that wartime experience, does anything come to mind as your most vivid memory?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: Nah. Just another day's work I think it was. You didn't have a chance to get scared to tell you the truth because everything was moving fast. But I didn't mind it a bit. After I was in there a while; you got used to it. And how the people were living, and how the civilians treated you, it wasn't too bad. But you know that's been 50 years ago. I don't remember a lot of that stuff. But I enjoyed it afterwards, but I wouldn't have volunteered. I wouldn't have volunteered; I had a kid. But that was the point. I had a wife and kid at home where just in life and everything had to take us away. I always kid my wife, you know, I was the only one of my buddies that didn't get drafted yet. I said I think you're the one that called the draft board and asked how come I didn't get drafted yet. I still kid her about that. She gets mad. No, we -- it was all right, though. I didn't mind it a bit, but I wouldn't volunteer for none of it again. Why the hell should I go fight there? I didn't need none of them islands.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Are you thankful you had the experience, though?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: Yeah, I'm glad I went now, but at the time I didn't want to go. But now that I was drafted and got in there, I didn't mind it a bit--well, because I come home okay.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Have any trouble adjusting when you came back?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: No. Just another day and new area. That's the way I figured it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Didn't have to deal with dreams?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: I didn't have no dreams. I was working and tired and sleeping. I didn't have time to dream.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was it like when you saw your daughter after?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: Beautiful. She used to look like Shirley Temple when she was a little kid. She's still a beautiful -- both of my daughters. One is 60 and the other is 55. Because I got drafted I didn't have the chance to get the other one in quicker. But I tell you, I have two beautiful daughters, never had no problems with them. I would be driving along and see these girls smoking on the street and I said to them, I don't mind you smoking when you're of age, but I don't want to ever catch you walking in the street with a cigarette in your mouth. That will never go with me. Go inside when you're smoking. I told them I don't want you to smoke outside, walking. It don't look good for a woman to do that. And I said if you do smoke, you are going to ruin your teeth and, boy, that cured them. They didn't smoke to this day, neither one of them smoke and they've got beautiful teeth but they look about 35 years old. They are nice looking girls, which I am proud of. I give my wife hell. I tell her if it wasn't for me they wouldn't be that good -- I'm the one that raised them. That makes her mad. See, we had a good life together, with the kids and all, we went all over, to California. I got five grandkids and three greatgrandkids, which is beautiful. The one greatgrand, five-years-old. She had an earache. They took her to the doctor. When the doctor was fooling around her ear, she seen blood and she said, "Oh my god, Mommy, get me out of here, they're trying to kill me." A little five-year-old kid saying that. How could she do a thing like that? I love those kids. When they call me, they say I'll call you again; I love you, Dad. That's what I like to hear. A lot of people don't have kids that say I love you. I don't know if you have kids or not.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I have one nine-year-old.

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: That's good. You got to have a kid.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You're probably one of the few guys overseas that had a kid, right?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: No. There was a few that had kids in our outfit.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was that a battalion?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: No, it was a company. We had survey and engineer survey, topographical -- make out these maps. Get in there, survey these areas.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you attached to any particular bigger unit?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: 43rd division.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: 43rd division?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: Yeah. But we never seen them. We were always on our own. We knew what we were doing because we had good commanders.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How big was your company?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: My company was about maybe a hundred. I don't know exactly, but it was a good size of them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You were responsible for setting up the sites where the artillery would move into?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: We had to go locate where they were firing from. Then call back and have artillery fire in at them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, so it was more like an artillery recon thing?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: I don't know what you would call it, but we would locate and call back and say send the artillery in. Sometimes you had to be--I thought I would have to run back a little further.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But they called you a surveyor because you were out there looking around?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: Topographical engineers they called us.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you were out there looking for enemy artillery?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: Oh, yeah. We had to locate the location and then have our -- have them bomb it out, clean it out.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Like a spotter or something?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Anything else?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: That's about it that I know of.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That covers it? No other memories jump out?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: None that I remember.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Sometimes after you start talking for a while, something comes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: Some of it coming back to us.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you go to the Hellregals(ph) dinner, does that bring back memories when you start talking about things?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: When I go to the reunion? Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Have you been to the Hellregals(ph) before?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: I've been there about five times. The owner that owns this apartment, her husband--they didn't have no kids. He was a sharp looking guy and he finally died. And we would always go and his wife would always buy me and another guy our tickets. That was nice. We got to go in there for nothing and eat. You see guys, you meet and all talking about different things. But I enjoyed the dinner. But they cut it out when he died. But she used to buy us tickets all the time. It never cost me a dime to go. She just bought tickets for the last one for two of us but her husband's dead now. Yeah, we would go to the reunions. I went to the last one, there were a lot of guys that we sat with--maybe they were dead or maybe they didn't go. I don't think -- those guys are disappearing. There were about six guys that we got acquainted with. I didn't see them there. I was just wondering if they died. But they were old -- about as old as my wife. She'll be 81 and she's worried about it. She's looking good. We've been married for 60 years.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Stillisano
sp.p: Some people don't last six months.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's right. I keep coming across veterans that didn't even know about their reunion organizations. One guy that was in my dad's division and I never see him on any list so they don't know he's out there. I'm going to send his name in so they can send him stuff.

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: They didn't send us nothing. You read it in the paper, too.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Exactly. I joined the division.

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: I like them because they have good food. We had good steak.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That was very nice.

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: And you got your drinks. That was petty reasonable. Of course, I didn't drink.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Stillisano
sp.p: Tommy likes a glass of wine once in a while, but that's it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You think that covers it?

sp.speaker: Thomas Stillisano
sp.p: Yeah. That's about it that I know of. END OF RECORDING ON CD.
